verses.1: A psalm of Asaph. Foreign nations have come into your inheritance, they have defiled your holy temple, they have made Jerusalem a place of waste.
verses.2: They have given the bodies of your servants to be food for the birds of the sky, the flesh of your faithful ones to the beasts of the earth.
verses.3: They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there is no one to bury them.
verses.4: We have become a disgrace to our neighbors, a laughingstock and a taunt to those around us.
verses.5: How long, O LORD, will you be angry forever? Will your fire of jealousy burn on and on?
verses.6: Pour out your wrath upon the nations who do not know you, and upon the kingdoms who have not called on your name.
verses.7: For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste to his dwelling.
verses.8: Do not remember against us the sins of our ancestors. Let your mercy come quickly to meet us, for we are brought very low.
verses.9: Help us, O God our savior, for the sake of the glory of your name. Deliver us and forgive our sins for the sake of your name.
verses.10: Let not the nations say, "Where is their God?" Let the nations see the vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been shed.
verses.11: Let the groaning of the prisoner come before you, according to the greatness of your power, rescue those doomed to death.
verses.12: Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their laps the shame they have heaped upon you, O Lord.
verses.13: But we are your people, the flock of your pasture. We will give thanks to you forever; from generation to generation we will proclaim your praise.

notes:
Notes
- v. 1: "a place of waste" ( Heb. עִיִּים) reflects the plural form used in the original, but it is rendered as a singular concept here for clarity.
- v. 10: "the vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been shed" — the Hebrew phrase is elliptical and context-dependent, and the translation aims to preserve the poetic and liturgical tone.
- v. 11: "those doomed to death" ( Heb. בְּנֵי תְמוּתָֽה) is a rare expression, possibly referring to those condemned or in perilous circumstances, and is interpreted accordingly.
